summary: Defines extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol that support the procedures of the Hierarchical PCE architecture from RFC 6805. This hierarchy lets path computation find good end-to-end paths across multiple domains.

plainLanguage.summary: When a trip crosses many regions, a main planner asks each regional planner for help. This gives them the words to talk to each other.

subtitle: The PCEP messages and fields that let a parent path computation server and its child servers plan one route across several network domains.

tldr.problem: A route that crosses several domains (IGP areas or autonomous systems) cannot be computed by one server that only sees its own domain, and the Hierarchical PCE architecture of RFC 6805 had no protocol encoding.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8685 adds new TLVs, objective function codes, metric types, an SVEC flag, an error type and NO-PATH flags to PCEP, so a child PCE can ask a parent PCE for a domain sequence or a full end-to-end path.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives H-PCE a wire format. It has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8685 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It is not obsoleted, so it remains the definition of the H-PCE PCEP extensions together with that update.

sections.title: Why a Hierarchy of Path Computation Elements
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) for a route and get the computed path back. RFC 6805 describes the Hierarchical PCE (H-PCE) architecture for computing end-to-end paths for inter-domain MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs. A parent PCE computes a multi-domain path from domain connectivity information. A child PCE covers one or more domains and computes the intra-domain part from its own topology.

The RFC lists the steps. The PCC sends an inter-domain request to its child PCE, which forwards it to the parent. The parent works out likely domain paths, asks the child PCEs along the way for intra-domain paths between border nodes, stitches the results together and returns the end-to-end path through the child PCE to the PCC.

The parent can also be asked for just the sequence of domains. The requester can then use per-domain computation (RFC 5152) or backward-recursive computation (RFC 5441) itself. This document only defines the PCEP extensions. Stateful operation, learning domain connectivity, choosing the destination domain and building the parent topology database are out of scope, and the RFC says applying H-PCE to very large groups of domains such as the Internet is not considered feasible or desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a road trip through several countries. A head planner decides which countries to cross, and a local planner in each country plans the roads inside it. This document is the language they use.

sections.title: What the Protocol Has to Express
sections.content:
Section 2 collects what PCEP must carry to support H-PCE. Requests need three new qualifications: a child PCE can ask the parent for a domain sequence only, a PCC can name the destination domain if it knows it, and a path can be forbidden from re-entering a domain.

Three new objective functions cover multi-domain goals: minimize the number of transit domains (MTD), minimize the number of border nodes (MBN) and minimize the number of common transit domains (MCTD). Two new metrics count the domains crossed and the border nodes crossed. A PCC may bound these to limit how many domains a path touches.

The RFC also needs a way to advertise the parent role during session setup, a way to identify PCE domains (an IGP area or an autonomous system), and support for domain diversity. Two paths are domain-diverse if they do not transit any of the same domains. The main motivation is avoiding fate-sharing, and it can also be used to avoid transit domains for security, geopolitical or commercial reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The planners need ways to say things like: only tell me which countries to cross, do not go through the same country twice, or use as few countries as possible. Two trips that must not share any country are called domain-diverse.

sections.title: Advertising Roles and Domains at Session Setup
sections.content:
Two optional TLVs go in the PCEP OPEN object. The H-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV (type 13, fixed length 4 octets) carries a 32-bit Flags field with one defined bit, P (Parent PCE Request). A child PCE MUST include the TLV and set P. A parent PCE MUST include it and leave P unset. In a PCC-to-child relationship neither side sets it. If both peers set P, session establishment MUST fail with a PCErr using Error-Type 1.

The Domain-ID TLV (type 14, variable length) tells the parent which domains a child PCE serves. Its Domain Type is 1 for a 2-byte AS number, 2 for a 4-byte AS number, 3 for a 4-byte OSPF area ID and 4 for an IS-IS area ID with a 2-byte Area-Len. If a PCE serves several domains, it includes one Domain-ID TLV for each.

A PCE that does not support the RFC ignores these TLVs, as RFC 5440 requires for unrecognized TLVs. It does not echo the capability TLV, so no H-PCE relationship is formed.
sections.plainLanguage: When two planners first meet they say who is the boss and which regions they look after. The boss says so with a special tick box, and if both tick it, they have to start over.

sections.title: Request Flags, Objective Functions, Metrics and Diversity
sections.content:
The H-PCE-FLAG TLV (type 15, length 4) rides in the RP object of a request. Bit D asks that the computed path not enter a domain more than once. Bit S says the child PCE wants only the domain sequence in the PCRep. Its presence means H-PCE path computation is requested. A Domain-ID TLV in the RP object gives the destination domain. If the destination is not actually in it, the parent should reply with a NO-PATH object.

The new OF codes are 12 (MTD), 13 (MBN) and 14 (MCTD). MCTD applies to a set of synchronized requests. The OF object may carry an OF-List TLV. Then the OF code in the object MUST be one of the H-PCE OFs, and the OF code in the list MUST NOT be, since it is the code the parent passes down for intra-domain computation. Otherwise the speaker MUST send Error-Type 10 with Error-Value 23.

The METRIC object gets two types: T=20 for Domain Count and T=21 for Border Node Count. If a domain is re-entered, it is counted twice. With the B-bit set the metric is a bound that must not be exceeded. With B cleared and C set it asks the PCE to optimize it.

For diversity, the SVEC object gets a Domain Diverse O-bit (bit 18). When set, the paths for the listed requests MUST NOT have any transit domains in common. Other diversity bits (link, node, SRLG) may still be set and apply in the shared ingress and egress domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A request can carry little switches such as: do not visit the same country twice, or just give me the list of countries. It can also say what to save on, such as the fewest countries or the fewest border crossings.

sections.title: Opening a Parent Session and Getting a Domain Sequence
sections.content:
To use a peer as its parent, a child PCE MUST set the P flag in the H-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in its Open message. It MAY also report its domain IDs in Domain-ID TLVs. The OF codes defined here can be placed in the OF-List TLV of the OPEN object to show which objective functions the PCE can implement, which helps a child choose a suitable parent.

If the child sends a request that needs a parent but the capability was never negotiated, the peer SHOULD answer with a PCErr using Error-Type 28 and Error-Value 1 (H-PCE Capability not advertised). If the peer does not want to act as parent for this child, it SHOULD answer with Error-Type 28 and Error-Value 2 (Parent PCE Capability cannot be provided).

To get only the domain sequence, the child sets the S bit in the H-PCE-FLAG TLV. If the parent succeeds, it returns the domain sequence in the ERO of a PCRep, using the domain subobjects of RFC 7897. Otherwise it returns a NO-PATH object.
sections.plainLanguage: The regional planner tells the head planner, you are my boss. If the head planner has not agreed to that, or does not want to, it answers with an error. A regional planner can also ask for just the list of countries to cross.

sections.title: Errors and Reasons for No Path
sections.content:
A PCE that can act as parent may not be configured or willing to do so for a given child. In that case the child gets a PCErr with Error-Type 28 (H-PCE Error) and a value of 1 or 2.

A parent can also fail to find a path or domain sequence. The RFC names three reasons: a child PCE cannot find a suitable path to the egress, the parent does not hear from a child PCE for a specified time, or the requested objective functions cannot be met. The parent MAY then send a negative PCRep with a NO-PATH object. Four new flags in the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV give the reason: bit 22 means the destination domain is unknown, bit 21 that one or more child PCEs are unresponsive, bit 20 that no resources are available in one or more domains, and bit 19 that the destination was not found in the indicated domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If the head planner cannot help, it says why: it does not know the destination country, a local planner did not answer, there is no room on the roads, or the place is not in that country.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
A child PCE must be configured with its parent's address and be authorized to peer with it. The RFC says discovery of parent-child relationships is not part of the architecture, because advertising or querying PCE locations across domain or provider boundaries is undesirable for security, scaling, commercial and confidentiality reasons. A parent PCE MUST only accept requests from authorized child PCEs and drop others. That means it MUST be able to cryptographically authenticate them. Multi-party shared-key schemes are not recommended between domains.

The security considerations of RFC 5440 are inherited. PCEP runs over TCP, so it can use TCP-AO or TLS. Multi-domain operation exchanges information across domain boundaries, which can be a confidentiality risk when different companies run the domains. PCEP lets each PCE keep its domain path information private using path-keys, and the architecture is designed to isolate domain topology as much as possible.

The RFC suggests that parent PCEs monitor counters such as child requests, successes and failures per peer, and requests from unauthorized child PCEs.
sections.plainLanguage: The head planner must only take calls from planners it trusts, and each region keeps its own map secret instead of handing it over.

messages.label: PCReq (inter-domain)
messages.note: Request goes to the child PCE for its domain.

messages.label: Intra-domain PCReq
messages.note: Sent to the child PCEs along the domain path.

fields.name: Flags (unassigned)
fields.desc: Set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Parent PCE Request bit: the child wishes to use the peer as its parent.

items.label: MTD
items.desc: Minimize the number of Transit Domains.

items.label: MBN
items.desc: Minimize the number of Border Nodes.

items.label: MCTD
items.desc: Minimize the number of Common Transit Domains across a set of paths.
